title: How to Keep Mice Out of Your Home and What to Do If They're Already Inside

seo.title: How to Keep Mice Out of the House—and What to Do Inside
seo.meta_description: Find and seal small gaps, secure food and trash, reduce nesting sites and clean droppings safely. Learn when recurring mouse signs need professional exclusion.
seo.search_intent: Prevent mice from entering, identify access routes and respond to indoor activity with exclusion, sanitation and safe cleanup rather than extermination-focused advice.

excerpt: To keep mice out, inspect and seal gaps around doors, pipes, vents and the foundation, store food and trash in closed containers and reduce easy nesting places. If you already have signs indoors, do not sweep or vacuum dry droppings; clean them using CDC disinfection precautions and get professional help if activity persists.
content_html:
A mouse usually does not get into a house because the front door happened to be open for a few seconds. More often, there is a permanent gap connecting the outdoors with a protected interior space. As long as that opening remains usable, new activity can continue even in a tidy home.

That is why the lasting fix starts with the building: find openings, reduce food and shelter, and close the routes that make entry easy. If there are already signs indoors, the response also needs to include safe cleanup and a plan that does not simply seal active animals into an inaccessible wall cavity.

First confirm where the activity is happening

Common clues include small droppings, gnaw marks, nighttime scratching in walls or ceilings, damaged food packaging and shredded material used for nesting.

You do not have to see a mouse to begin investigating. Look at where the signs concentrate. Droppings under a kitchen sink point you toward plumbing penetrations. Signs in a pantry make food storage and cabinet gaps worth checking. Noise in an attic or ceiling shifts the inspection toward upper-level vents, eaves and utility openings.

If there are large amounts of droppings, nesting material or widespread contamination, do not disturb it dry. Heavy infestations require additional cleanup precautions.

The openings that matter are surprisingly small

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) notes that mice can fit through a hole about 1/4 inch, roughly 6 millimeters, wide. That changes what a useful inspection looks like. Checking only whether the doors close is not enough.

Look inside and outside around:

  • pipes beneath sinks and washing machines;
  • electrical, water, gas and sewer penetrations;
  • floor-to-wall joints;
  • door and window frames;
  • vents and grilles;
  • garages, basements, crawl spaces and attics;
  • foundation, siding, roofline, eaves and soffits.

Daylight through a gap, rub marks or repeated signs near one penetration can help you decide where to focus first.

Seal gaps with materials that create a real barrier

The right repair depends on the size and construction. CDC suggests steel wool held in place with caulk for small holes and more durable materials such as metal mesh, sheet metal or cement for larger openings.

The goal is a physical repair, not a cosmetic plug. A gap around a pipe should not become an entry route again as soon as a soft surface material degrades.

Replace damaged weatherstripping and address door gaps too. In a garage or utility room, a visible strip under a door may be a much more important route than a tiny crack elsewhere.

If mice are clearly inside, do not seal blindly

Exclusion is essential for preventing new entries, but the order matters when there is definite indoor activity. Closing every apparent exit without a plan can leave animals inside walls, closets or other enclosed spaces.

If you cannot tell how many animals are present, where they move or whether they are using wall cavities, ask a qualified pest or wildlife professional for an inspection-and-exclusion plan. You can specifically request an approach that prioritizes structural barriers and prevention.

In attached homes and apartment buildings, routes may cross shared walls and utility chases. A landlord or building manager may need to address spaces outside your individual unit.

Make the indoors less rewarding

Mice use food, water and nesting material. Store dry foods in sturdy containers with tight lids, clean spills and crumbs promptly and keep household trash in a container that closes securely.

Pet food matters too. Store bags securely and avoid leaving food accessible overnight when it is not needed. Bird seed, livestock feed and bulk grain in garages or sheds deserve the same treatment.

Reduce piles of paper, cardboard and textiles in areas where you have found signs. Decluttering does not repair an entry hole, but it removes protected nesting areas and makes new evidence much easier to spot.

The outside of the house is part of the system

Review trash, compost, seed, animal feed and dense storage immediately around the building. Secure containers and avoid leaving dependable food sources right beside potential entry points.

Wood piles, stored objects and thick vegetation against the foundation can also create sheltered routes. You do not need a bare yard; the practical goal is to reduce cover and food directly beside the structure.

Do not sweep or vacuum dry mouse droppings

This is a safety issue, not just a cleaning preference. CDC warns that sweeping or vacuuming rodent urine, droppings or nesting material before disinfection can put contaminated particles into the air.

For a small amount, ventilate as CDC recommends, wear rubber or plastic gloves and thoroughly wet the material with an appropriate household disinfectant. Follow the product's contact-time directions, wipe the material up with paper towels and disinfect the surrounding hard surface.

Do not mix cleaning chemicals. If contamination is extensive, nests are widespread, the building has been closed for a long time or rodents have entered heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) ducts, follow CDC's additional precautions or get professional help before disturbing the area.

How to tell whether the problem is actually improving

Once old signs have been safely cleaned, watch for new droppings, fresh gnawing or recurring noises. Removing the old evidence first makes it possible to distinguish current activity from something that happened weeks ago.

Not seeing a mouse for one evening is less meaningful than seeing no new signs over a sustained period. Mice are discreet and much of their activity occurs while the home is quiet.

When to bring in a professional

Get help if new droppings continue after obvious food and entry issues have been addressed, you hear activity inside walls or ductwork, the access area cannot be reached safely or contamination is extensive.

Professional help is also reasonable when small children, pets or vulnerable household members make the situation harder to manage safely. Explain that you want an inspection-and-exclusion approach that corrects the building conditions and reduces future entry.

The durable solution is at the boundary of the home

Once a house has had mouse activity, make the exterior inspection part of maintenance. Recheck weatherstripping, utility penetrations, vent screens and older repairs periodically, especially after construction or seasonal changes.

The goal is not to turn the house into a fortress against one animal. It is to remove the small connections that make a warm, dry indoor space with food easy to reach. Once those connections are gone, the solution no longer depends on what happens to each individual mouse.

faq.question: How small a hole can a mouse get through?
faq.answer: CDC says mice can fit through openings about 1/4 inch, roughly 6 mm, so inspect pipe penetrations, doors, vents and building joints carefully.

faq.question: Should I vacuum mouse droppings?
faq.answer: Not while they are dry. CDC recommends wetting droppings with disinfectant first and following its cleanup procedure so contaminated particles are not put into the air.

faq.question: What attracts mice to a house?
faq.answer: Food, water and nesting shelter matter, but small structural openings that make the interior easy to enter are a major part of the problem.

faq.question: When should I call a professional?
faq.answer: When signs persist, activity is inside walls or ducts, contamination is extensive, or you cannot identify and close the route safely.
